profiles.meeting_scenario: A government health technology assessment agency is conducting a design review of a draft 'Public and Patient Involvement in HTA' framework before it is submitted to the executive committee for approval and used in a six-month pilot. The meeting is between the framework's methods owner and the patient partnership lead to check whether the draft is ready, identify any missing implementation details, and confirm what will be carried into the pilot package. The agenda is to review where involvement occurs across the HTA lifecycle, how participant recruitment and orientation are described, what counts as representative input for pilot cases, and how the framework handles communication back to contributors. The expected outcome is a shared decision to approve the draft with light revisions and send it forward as 'pilot-ready' for the next HTA cycle.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: HTA process design, evidence appraisal, committee governance, methodological standardization
members.background: A health economist who has spent nine years inside the agency refining appraisal workflows and template-based review processes across drugs, devices, and care pathways.
members.private_state: She wants the framework approved with minimal disruption to existing HTA timelines, and is concerned that adding open-ended engagement steps will create delays the appraisal units cannot absorb during the pilot.
hidden_assumptions: In the HTA context, 'early involvement' naturally means after a topic has already entered the work programme but before the evidence protocol is finalized.
A pilot is implementation-ready if internal governance, decision templates, and reviewer instructions are stable enough for one live assessment to test them.
Patient input is 'representative' when recurring themes are captured reliably, even if not every subgroup appears directly in the contributor pool.
A 'feedback loop' is fulfilled once contributors receive a plain-language account of how the final recommendation used their input.
Participant orientation can rely on the agency's existing standard onboarding for external committee contributors unless the framework explicitly says otherwise.

members.name: Maya Chen
members.role: Patient Partnership and Public Engagement Manager
members.expertise: Patient engagement design, community recruitment, accessibility, contributor support, equity-focused participation
members.background: A former nonprofit engagement director who joined the agency three years ago to build patient-facing participation practices across consultation and advisory activities.
members.private_state: She wants the framework to establish a credible engagement model that communities will trust, and is worried that a narrow operational interpretation will produce token involvement while still being labeled a success.
hidden_assumptions: Involvement is only 'early' if patients can shape which questions enter the HTA and how the workplan is framed before scoping is largely set.
A pilot is not truly ready unless participant-facing materials, reimbursement instructions, and support steps are workable for real contributors across more than one case type.
Input is only 'representative' enough for the framework if key affected communities, including equity-relevant groups, are visibly present rather than inferred from general themes.
A proper 'feedback loop' includes updates during the process when patient input changes framing, not only a final summary after recommendations are issued.
When a document says the agency will use the 'standard orientation,' it includes plain-language preparation, glossary support, and a live prep conversation tailored for nontechnical contributors.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both endorse 'bringing patients in early' in the HTA process.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means patient contributors are engaged at the scoping stage, after the topic has already been selected for assessment but before the protocol and comparators are locked.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means patient and public contributors can influence topic framing even before formal scoping, including priority-setting and initial question formation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as advocating for involvement well before the final recommendation, and 'early' sounds sufficiently aligned in a design review without prompting either to name the exact HTA milestone.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'representative input' means for the pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the pilot should test whether the framework can gather 'representative patient input.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks representation is achieved if the pilot captures stable patient experience themes from a small number of contributors and triangulates them with published qualitative evidence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks representation requires direct participation from distinct affected groups, such as rural patients, caregivers, and historically underserved communities, even if thematic overlap exists.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a shared quality bar, and because neither wants to reopen sample design in a review meeting, each treats their own standard as the obvious operational meaning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the framework needs a clear 'feedback loop' for contributors.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes only final-stage communication: a concise explanation of how contributor input informed the completed HTA recommendation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes process-stage communication as well: updates on how input affected scoping decisions, what was not used, and a final summary at the end.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both think feedback is obviously necessary and use the same phrase, but the framework section title is broad enough that neither notices the other has drawn a different boundary around which communications are included.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both accept the draft sentence saying contributors will receive the agency's 'standard orientation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means the existing 45-minute virtual onboarding used for external committee participants, focused on confidentiality, conflicts, and the HTA timeline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means a tailored participant support package: plain-language pre-read, glossary, reimbursement instructions, accessibility check, and a preparatory call before the formal session.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase refers to an established internal practice, so both treat it as already settled; because each works with a different 'standard' in daily operations, the discrepancy stays invisible.

turns.inner_thought: I need this review to land cleanly. The executive committee wants something they can approve without reopening process design, and the appraisal teams cannot absorb a lot of new moving parts before the next cycle. For me, pilot-ready means governance is settled, the templates are stable, reviewer instructions are usable, and we can run one live assessment through without destabilizing timelines. If we stay focused on light revisions, we can keep this on track.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Maya. I was hoping we could use this hour to confirm that the framework is pilot-ready for the next HTA cycle, and just identify any light revisions we need before it goes up to executive.

turns.inner_thought: I can work with a light-touch review as long as 'pilot-ready' actually means contributors can participate without confusion or feeling used. I do not want us declaring success on the basis of a process that looks neat internally but feels tokenistic from the outside. For me, readiness includes participant-facing materials, support, reimbursement steps, and something credible across more than one kind of case, even if I don't push that too hard right now.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, I mainly want to make sure it's genuinely workable for real contributors and that what we're describing reads as authentic involvement, not just symbolic consultation.

turns.inner_thought: The draft now places patients after a topic is already in the work programme but before the evidence protocol and comparators are locked. That is early enough to shape the scoping pack without creating a new pre-programme engagement layer. If she is comfortable with the phrase 'involved early,' we should be fine.
turns.utterance: One area I think has improved is the lifecycle section. We now say patients will be involved early, and the way it's written makes clear that this happens while the scope is still being formed so the key questions can still be shaped.

turns.inner_thought: Good, because early involvement has to mean people can influence framing before the agency has effectively decided what matters. I still read that section as leaving room for patient and public voices before scoping hardens, including how the work is initially framed. If that's the shared understanding, then the language is moving in the right direction.
turns.utterance: Yes, I was pleased to see that too. Early involvement is really important if we want people to have a genuine chance to influence the framing before the agency gets too far into defining what will be assessed.

turns.inner_thought: The pilot will only be credible if it visibly includes the groups most affected, not just a couple of articulate contributors whose themes happen to overlap with others. I want rural patients, caregivers, and underserved communities to be present in some identifiable way. I'll keep it at the level of 'representative patient input' so we don't get pulled into a sample design fight right now.
turns.utterance: On recruitment, I think the pilot will only be convincing if it can show the framework is capable of gathering representative patient input across the populations affected by a case.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed in principle, but we have to keep this proportionate. For the pilot, I'd be satisfied if the main patient experience themes come through reliably from a manageable number of contributors and line up with the published qualitative literature. We do not need to build a large recruitment exercise for every subgroup in six months. As long as the draft leaves room for a practical approach, I can support the wording.
turns.utterance: I agree, representative patient input is an important test for the pilot. We should be able to show that the main patient themes come through consistently, while still keeping the recruitment approach manageable for the teams.

turns.inner_thought: I'm glad the communication section stayed concise. For me, a clear feedback loop means that once the recommendation is completed, contributors get a plain-language explanation of how their input was considered. That's enough to close the loop without adding extra process checkpoints that the units will struggle to maintain during a live assessment.
turns.utterance: The other change I was glad to see is in the communications section. The framework now includes a clear feedback loop, which is important so contributors can see where their perspectives landed in the recommendation.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and I also need that feedback loop to operate during the process, not just at the end. Trust comes from hearing what happened to your input as the review evolves, especially when something wasn't taken forward. I think the heading is broad enough to cover those updates, so I don't need to unpack it unless someone narrows it.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. A strong feedback loop will help with trust as well, because people need to hear back as the work evolves and understand how their comments affected the review process.

turns.inner_thought: The implementation appendix is better now that it references the standard orientation. I am reading that as the usual participant support package my team has been building into public-facing activities: plain-language prep, glossary help, reimbursement guidance, accessibility checks, and a live prep conversation. If that is already named as standard, we may not need to spell every element out in the framework itself.
turns.utterance: I also thought the implementation appendix looked stronger once it said all contributors would receive the agency's standard orientation before they take part.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, using the standard orientation is exactly what keeps this practical. The existing 45-minute virtual onboarding for external committee contributors is already in place and doesn't require building a parallel process. If we make only minor wording edits today, I can take this forward as ready for one live pilot case without creating timeline risk.
turns.utterance: I agree. Using the agency's standard orientation keeps the pilot practical, and with that in place I think we're very close. If we tidy a few points of wording, I'd be comfortable sending this forward as pilot-ready.
